title: The Rhetorical Situation
short: The writer, the audience, the purpose, the context (the occasion and the need that calls for the text) and the message shape every choice a writer makes.
trouble: Learners analyze a text without asking who it was for and when it was written, and so misjudge its choices.

blocks.html: In What Rhetoric Is you saw that every text is written for someone, for a reason. The rhetorical situation names all the pieces that shape a text, so you can see why the writer chose what they chose.

head: Part
Ask
Example: a student’s letter asking for longer library hours
rows: Who is writing, and what do readers know about them?
a junior who studies in the library after practice
Who will read it? What do they care about and already believe?
the principal, who worries about staffing costs
What should change in the reader’s mind or actions?
keep the library open until 6:00 during exam weeks
When and where? What problem calls for this text?
two weeks before finals; the library now closes at 4:00
a polite request, a short plan, an offer to help
blocks.cap: The five parts of the rhetorical situation.

blocks.html: The rhetorician Lloyd Bitzer, in a 1968 essay called “The Rhetorical Situation,” said a situation starts with an exigence: a problem or need that words can help change. It also has an audience that can act, and constraints (beliefs, facts, rules) that limit what the writer can say. Richard Vatz answered in 1973 that speakers help make situations, by choosing which problems to call urgent. Scholars still discuss both views, and both are useful: ask what called for the text, and ask how the writer framed it.

blocks.name: wr-triangle

fill.writer: President Lincoln, in the Civil War
fill.audience: the crowd, and the nation reading the papers
fill.purpose: honor the dead; recommit the living

blocks.cap: The Gettysburg Address in its situation.

blocks.html: Before you write or analyze, ask five questions: Who is writing? To whom? Why? When and where, in answer to what? What is said, and how? Every choice in a text is fitted to those answers.

The same words can be wise in one situation and foolish in another. “Students are exhausted” is a strong opening for a principal who already worries about exam stress, and a weak one for a board focused on the budget. You can’t judge a choice until you know what it was fitted to.

blocks.title: Lincoln at Gettysburg
blocks.q: Why is the Gettysburg Address so short (about 272 words)? Use the situation.
steps: Context: the cemetery’s organizers invited Lincoln to give “a few appropriate remarks” after the main speaker.
The main speaker, Edward Everett, a famous orator, spoke for about two hours first.
Audience: a crowd that had already heard a long oration, and newspaper readers across the North.
So brevity was fitting: a short, formal dedication, not a second long speech.
blocks.a: The invitation, the program and the tired audience all called for a short speech; Lincoln fit his words to the occasion.

blocks.title: Douglass in Rochester
blocks.q: On July 5, 1852, Frederick Douglass spoke at Corinthian Hall in Rochester, New York, invited by the Rochester Ladies’ Anti-Slavery Society to speak about the Fourth of July. Name the parts of the situation.
steps: Writer: Douglass, a famous speaker and editor who had escaped from slavery.
Audience: about 500 to 600 listeners, many of them already opposed to slavery.
Context: Independence Day, while slavery was legal in much of the country and the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 required Northern help in returning people who had escaped.
Purpose: make an audience that already agreed with him feel the full weight of celebrating liberty while slavery went on.
blocks.a: A friendly audience, a patriotic holiday and a harsh new law: that situation explains why Douglass could be blunt instead of cautious.

blocks.html: Analyzing a text without asking who it was for and when it was written. A reader who calls the Gettysburg Address “too short to say much” has missed that Lincoln was asked for a few remarks after a two-hour oration. Check: before you judge any choice, write one sentence each for the writer, audience, purpose and context.
